transcription.tex: In \(3^5\), 3 is the base and 5 is the exponent (or index). The whole expression is a power.\par Use precise language: when multiplying powers with the same base, add the indices.
\[6x^2+10x^3-4x+x^3=11x^3+6x^2-4x\]\par Take care with the positive \(x^3\) term.
\[\frac{x^3}{3x^2}-\frac{2x}{3x^2}=\frac{x}{3}-\frac2{3x}\]\par Split a fraction across terms in its numerator, never its denominator.

transcription.tex: \textbf{2. MAT 2007 1E}\quad For integers \(x,n\), consider\[(1-x)^n(2-x)^{2n}(3-x)^{3n}(4-x)^{4n}(5-x)^{5n}\]Which statement holds?\par A. Negative when \(n>5\) and \(x<5\).\par B. Negative when \(n\) is odd and \(x>5\).\par C. Negative when \(n\) is a multiple of 3 and \(x>5\).\par D. Negative when \(n\) is even and \(x<5\).
B. If \(x>5\), all five bases are negative. The combined sign is \((-1)^{15n}\), which is negative when \(n\) is odd.

transcription.tex: Factorising reverses expanding: write an expression as a product of factors.
\[x(x+1)(x+2)\]Factorised: a product of three linear factors. A linear expression has the form \(ax+b\).
\[x(x+1)+(x-1)(x+1)\]Not yet factorised: the outermost operation is addition.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Recap}\par For \(x^2+bx+c\), find two numbers that add to \(b\) and multiply to \(c\). The coefficient is the number multiplying a term.
\textbf{When the coefficient of \(x^2\) is not 1}\par Guess and check the brackets, or split the middle term.
\textbf{Split the middle term}\quad Find two numbers with sum \(5\) and product \(2(-12)=-24\).
\textbf{Working}\quad Use those numbers to split \(5x\), then factorise both pairs.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Challenge · MAT 2007 1A}\quad For integers \(r,s\), when is this expression an integer?\[\frac{6^{r+s}12^{r-s}}{8^r9^{r+2s}}\]Choose: \(r+s\le0\), \(s\le0\), \(r\le0\), or \(r\ge s\).
\[\frac{2^{3r-s}3^{2r}}{2^{3r}3^{2r+4s}}=2^{-s}3^{-4s}=162^{-s}\]\par This is an integer precisely when \(s\le0\).

transcription.tex: A surd is a root that does not simplify to a rational number. A rational number can be written \(a/b\), where \(a,b\) are integers and \(b\ne0\).\[\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab},\qquad\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}=\sqrt{\frac ab}\quad(a\ge0,b>0)\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{3}\quad Simplify \(\sqrt{75}-\sqrt{12}\) in the form \(a\sqrt3\), with \(a\) an integer.
Each equals \(\sqrt{n+1}-\sqrt n\). Rationalising gives \(1/(\sqrt{n+1}+\sqrt n)\), which decreases as \(n\) increases.\par The largest \(n\) is 99, so the smallest is \(10-3\sqrt{11}\).

\textbf{2. SMC 2012 Q21}\quad Which has no square root of the form \(x+y\sqrt2\), with positive integers \(x,y\)?\[\begin{gathered}17+12\sqrt2;\quad22+12\sqrt2;\quad38+12\sqrt2;\\54+12\sqrt2;\quad73+12\sqrt2\end{gathered}\]
Squaring gives \(x^2+2y^2+2xy\sqrt2\), so \(xy=6\).\par The pairs \((1,6),(2,3),(3,2),(6,1)\) give constants \(73,22,17,38\).\par Therefore the answer is \(54+12\sqrt2\).

transcription.tex: What can we multiply this surd by to obtain a rational number?
Rationalising a denominator makes it rational. Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero expression, so the value stays unchanged.
This gives a simpler denominator and makes expressions involving surds easier to combine.

transcription.tex: Writing surds in power form is useful in later calculus questions.
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{4+4\sqrt x+x}{x}&=\frac{4+4x^{1/2}+x}{x}\\&=4x^{-1}+4x^{-1/2}+1\end{aligned}\]\par Expand, replace roots with powers, then split the fraction.
\textbf{Test your understanding}\quad Express \(\frac{(x+\sqrt x)^2}{2\sqrt x}\) as powers of \(x\).
